# Two scripts with the same letters in parallel Unicode names: Devanagari, in which Sanskrit is printed today, and
# Brahmi, the script of Ashoka's edicts (3rd century BCE), ancestor of the scripts of South and Southeast Asia.
# Values are IAST; Harvard-Kyoto capitals also work (A I U for long vowels, T D N S M H for ṭ ḍ ṇ ṣ ṃ ḥ). engine=abugida:
# a consonant carries a short a; another vowel is written as a sign on it; consonants with no vowel between them join.

column4: Sanskrit was handed down by memory for centuries before it was written; it has been written in many scripts, from Brahmi to Devanagari, in which each consonant carries a vowel a unless a sign changes it.

column2: The script in which Sanskrit is printed today, used from about the 11th century in northern India; the line along the top joins the letters of a word.

Type in IAST (the usual romanisation: ā, ś, ṛ …) or with capitals for the dotted letters (A I U, T D N S, M H). A consonant carries a short a; type the next vowel to change it, or another consonant to join them. On the keys: tap a consonant, then a vowel. | and || are the full stops.

column2: The oldest script of India that can be read, known from the edicts of the emperor Ashoka (about 260 BCE), cut on rocks and polished pillars; nearly every script of South and Southeast Asia comes from it.

The same letters as Devanagari in the shapes of Ashoka’s time. Type in IAST or with Harvard-Kyoto capitals; a consonant carries a short a, the next vowel changes it, and consonants without a vowel between them join.
